section_summary: This section contains U.S. diplomatic reporting on Japanese wartime production, food supply, finance, transportation, and resource development across Japan and occupied Asia, much of it translated from monitored broadcasts. It also includes Roy Hoko Ikeda’s proposals for postwar Japanese government and international relations, and correspondence about exchanging intelligence on Japanese shipping and oil production. The section begins and ends within longer translated broadcast reports.

subfiles.title: Economic items from Japanese broadcasts, concluding pages
subfiles.about: Reports Japanese wartime economic measures across occupied Asia.
subfiles.summary: The surviving pages cover rubber, cotton, banks, transport, North China minerals, Southeast Asian oil and shipbuilding, Hong Kong reconstruction, Chinese industry, river works, food policy, Korean rice, and Indochinese customs. Page 197 repeats page 196. The compilation began before this section.

subfiles.title: Economic materials from monitored Japanese broadcasts, telegram 554 section one
subfiles.to: Secretary of State; Board of Economic Warfare
subfiles.about: Summarizes Japanese broadcasts on rice, Manchurian industry, shipbuilding, Philippine fuel and cotton.
subfiles.summary: Reports Japan’s 1942 rice crop, Manchurian iron and industrial budgets, shipbuilding in Kwantung and Davao, Philippine butanol production, and Luzon cotton estimates.

subfiles.title: Economic materials from monitored Japanese broadcasts, telegram 554 section two
subfiles.to: Secretary of State; Board of Economic Warfare
subfiles.about: Continues the broadcast summary with Southeast Asian production, shipping, transport and occupied China.
subfiles.summary: Covers Celebes fish and cotton, Singapore shipping, Indochinese timber and roads, Burma teak, transfer of Allied property, Japanese advisers, tung oil, and Shanghai silk purchasing.

subfiles.title: Japanese-Chinese Economic Conference in Tokyo
subfiles.about: Points to a despatch on Tojo’s opening address at the Japanese-Chinese Economic Conference.
subfiles.summary: References despatch 9670 concerning the conference and Tojo’s policy toward occupied China.

subfiles.title: Economic materials from monitored Japanese broadcasts, telegram 605 section one
subfiles.to: Secretary of State; Board of Economic Warfare
subfiles.about: Summarizes broadcasts on Japanese crop prices, industrial policy, war bonds, and North China transport.
subfiles.summary: Reports rice purchase prices, war bonds, magnesium production, commodity subsidies, food cultivation, North China rail and pier statistics, wheat flour shipments, and radiogram service.

subfiles.title: Economic materials from monitored Japanese broadcasts, telegram 605 section two
subfiles.to: Secretary of State; Board of Economic Warfare
subfiles.about: Continues the broadcast summary on steel, freight, Philippine agriculture, Java cotton and Indochinese transport.
subfiles.summary: Describes Qingdao blast furnaces, bonded freight transport, a Mengchiang power plant, Hong Kong trade, Philippine cotton and derris root, Java gutta-percha and cotton, and reduced Saigon–Hanoi trains.

subfiles.title: Reference on Roy Hoko Ikeda’s postwar proposals
subfiles.about: Summarizes Ikeda’s proposals for Japanese democracy, colonial self-government and international institutions.
subfiles.summary: Notes reforms to the emperor’s role, colonial representation and plebiscites, Asian self-government, regional councils, and international policing.

subfiles.title: Letter from Roy Hoko Ikeda to Sumner Welles
subfiles.about: Submits Ikeda’s postwar proposals and comments on Japanese public opinion and an incident at the Utah relocation center.
subfiles.summary: Ikeda asks Welles to read and comment on his proposals. His postscript criticizes a State Department representative’s response after military police shot two evacuees at the relocation center.

subfiles.title: Skeleton Idea of the Post-War Japan’s Political and Economic Structure and Her International Relation
subfiles.about: Sets out a proposed democratic monarchy, cooperative economy, colonial self-government and international government.
subfiles.summary: Ikeda proposes removing reactionary institutions around the emperor, democratizing the Diet, extending women’s suffrage, and protecting civil liberties. He advocates joint worker and capitalist management of major industries, agricultural cooperatives, and colonial self-government leading to independence. He also proposes regional councils and an international government with policing and transport authority.

subfiles.title: Acknowledgment to Roy Hoko Ikeda
subfiles.about: Acknowledges receipt of Ikeda’s letter and postwar proposals.
subfiles.summary: Thanks Ikeda for sending his views on postwar reorganization in Japan and the Far East.

subfiles.title: Economic materials from monitored Japanese broadcasts, telegram 639
subfiles.to: Secretary of State; Board of Economic Warfare
subfiles.about: Summarizes broadcasts on North China food and railways, Japanese savings and industrial production.
subfiles.summary: Reports food shortages and ration changes, Zhejiang railway repairs, Japanese savings and investment, industrial associations, coal output, Chinese commodity exchange plans, small vessel building, and a claimed welding advance.

subfiles.title: Despatch 1049 forwarding translated Japanese broadcasts
subfiles.about: Forwards fuller translations of broadcasts summarized in telegram 355.
subfiles.summary: Transmits monitored economic broadcasts for March 1–10, 1943, to the Board of Economic Warfare.

subfiles.title: Economic items selected from Japanese and Nanking regime broadcasts, March 1–10
subfiles.to: U.S. Embassy, Chungking; Board of Economic Warfare
subfiles.about: Compiles monitored broadcasts on food, crops, resources, transportation and banking.
subfiles.summary: The enclosure reports Shanghai rations and prices, Japan’s 1943–44 crop targets, and plans for South Seas fiber, oil, food and local processing. It also covers Manchurian afforestation, Indochinese air service, Lower Yangtze material controls, Peking food supplies, Burma reconstruction, and a Bank of Japan loan to the Federal Reserve Bank of China.

subfiles.title: Telegram 686 on exchanging economic intelligence with General Wang
subfiles.to: Secretary of State; Board of Economic Warfare
subfiles.about: Requests U.S. shipping and petroleum intelligence to exchange with Wang Peng Sheng.
subfiles.summary: Boehringer reports Wang’s requests for Japanese shipping losses and construction capacity, oil imports, and production and damage data for the Netherlands East Indies and Borneo. Wang may provide intelligence on Japan and a North Pacific report.

subfiles.title: Paraphrase of telegram 686
subfiles.about: Restates the request to exchange shipping and oil intelligence with Wang Peng Sheng.
subfiles.summary: A typed paraphrase of telegram 686 details Wang’s requests for Japanese shipping figures and oil data from the Netherlands East Indies and North Borneo.

subfiles.title: Reply on economic intelligence exchange with General Wang
subfiles.from: Department of State; Board of Economic Warfare
subfiles.about: Authorizes a controlled exchange and supplies petroleum figures while withholding shipping data pending clearance.
subfiles.summary: The Board of Economic Warfare supports an embassy-led exchange, subject to military attaché clearance. It supplies prewar Netherlands East Indies and Borneo oil production, refining and damage estimates, requests information on synthetic fuel and rehabilitation, and says shipping figures await Navy clearance.

subfiles.title: Despatch 1081 forwarding translated Japanese broadcasts
subfiles.about: Forwards fuller translations of broadcasts summarized in telegram 449.
subfiles.summary: Transmits monitored economic broadcasts for March 11–24, 1943, to the Board of Economic Warfare.

subfiles.title: Economic items selected from Japanese and Nanking regime broadcasts, March 11–24
subfiles.to: U.S. Embassy, Chungking; Board of Economic Warfare
subfiles.about: Reports economic and infrastructure measures in occupied China, Manchuria, Sumatra, Burma and the Philippines.
subfiles.summary: The enclosure describes eased material movement restrictions in Central China, mineral production quotas in Manchuria, and Japanese accounts of Sumatra’s resources and reconstruction. It continues with a power plant, Burma’s food and mineral resources, Philippine telephone and telegraph expansion, and Grand Canal and Yellow River works. The report continues beyond page 253.
